newsitem.title: UK: Small gas projects blossom with kinder contracts.
newsitem.headline: Small gas projects blossom with kinder contracts.

text.p: Small-scale natural gas projects are blooming across the globe, despite their apparent unattractiveness compared to oil, because of host governments' growing willingness to sign more generous contracts, a leading consultancy said on Monday.
"A quiet revolution has been taking place around the world: the development of small gas discoveries in new markets," Geneva's Petroconsultants said in a report.

Governments are recognising poor gas field economics relative to oil in their exploration and production (E&P) contracts and this "has clearly encouraged the development of gas in many new countries to the extent where small but significant markets have been established," the report said.
Gas E&P involves greater investment in infrastructure such as pipelines, project development times are generally longer, and the price of gas at the wellhead is generally lower.

"The economics of upstream gas development...compare far less favourably than similarly sized oil projects," Petroconsultants said. "It is for these reasons that exploration in gas prone areas has, for many decades, been avoided by most E&P eompanies."
Larger gas producers, however, tend to allow investors acceptable returns despite relatively harsh fiscal contract terms because of generally lower costs and lower risk.
But smaller fields are now being opened up where the costs and the risk are higher.

United Meridien Corp., for example, has signed a gas sales contract with Cote d'Ivoire which provides for a gas price of $1.50-$1.67 per milion British Thermal Units (BTU), equivalent to some $9-$10 a barrel. That is about half the current oil price.
The average cashflow the state receives from a small project can be 10-20 percentage points less for gas than for oil.

In Indonesia, the state take for oil projects is 87 percent of gross cashflow compared with 64 percent for gas, the report said, while in Peru it is 73 percent for oil compared with 59 percent for gas.

Argentina, which offers mostly small gas discoveries a long way from markets, has one of the top ten most lenient fiscal regimes in Petroconsultants' study and this has been a significant factor in the recent declaration by the country's largest gas producer that it would more than double annual gas sales to 23 billion cubic metres by 2004.
But not all government contracts take account of the poorer economics for gas fields.
"The average state take from gas projects in many countries at best remains on a par with that from oil and, in 10 percent of the regimes surveyed, is significantly higher.
"If future exploration is to be enticed into gas-prone areas where the market remain underdeveloped the government clearly has a role to play."
